questions_and_answers.question: In Hindi, how do you mark a verb participle when it is used as an adjective?

answers.answer: By adding the post‑position को after the participle

questions_and_answers.question: If a verb cannot agree with any subject or direct‑case noun, what form does it take by default?

articles.text:
Hindi grammar builds on structures you already know — nouns, adjectives, pronouns, postpositions, verbs and other parts of speech.  Phrases such as subjects, direct and indirect objects, adverbial and adjectival phrases combine into clauses, and clauses combine into sentences.  Most unfamiliar structures are simply combinations of familiar elements.  This unit introduces several combinations that are common in both spoken and written Hindi.

**Participles as adjectives**

Verb participles can act as adjectives when a form of **हुआ** is added.  With present or imperfective participles, examples include: **सोती हुई लड़की** (the sleeping girl) and **बहता हुआ पानी** (the flowing water).  With past or perfective participles, examples include: **टूटा हुआ बटन** (a broken button), **बैठा हुआ आदमी** (the seated man), **आपकी लिखी हुई किताब** (the book which you wrote) and **मेरी कल की पहनी हुई जुराबें** (the socks I wore yesterday).

These adjectival phrases can also function adverbially when put in the oblique singular masculine form: **बैठे हुए** “taking a seat,” **साड़ी पहनते हुए** “while dressing,” **साड़ियां पहनते हुए** “wearing saris” and **टाई पहने हुए** “wearing a necktie.”  Repeating the adverb emphasises continuity: **चलते चलते** means “walking constantly” and **हँसते हँसते** means “laughing constantly.”  Expressions such as **मरते मरते** and **गिरते गिरते** mean “on the brink of dying” and “on the brink of falling.”

**No verb ‘have’**

Hindi lacks a verb equivalent to English “have.”  Possession of relatives, body parts and other inalienable things is expressed with a possessive adjective or a **का‑phrase**, for example **उनके दो बच्चे हैं** (“They have two children”) or **उसकी एक आँख है** (“He has one eye”).  To express maladies you say there is something in or on the body: **मेरे सिर में दर्द है** literally “There’s pain in my head.”  Other ailments use **को**: **मुझको जुकाम है** (“I have a cold”), **मुझको बुखार था** (“I had a fever”).  Ownership of movable property is shown with **पास**, as in **मेरे पास दो गाड़ियां थीं**, **उनके पास एक बड़ा सुंदर कुत्ता था**, **मेरे दोस्त के पास बड़ा अच्छा ड्राइवर है**, **हमारे पास अपना घर नहीं होगा** and **क्या आप लोगों के पास रहने के लिये बड़े‑बड़े मकान हैं?**

**Combining verbs with कर**

When two or more verbs share a subject, the endings of all but the last verb can be replaced by the special marker **कर** (or **के**/ **करके**).  For example, **जाइये देखिये** becomes **जाकर देखिये** (“Go and see”), and **खाना खाइये और वापस आइये** becomes **खाना खाकर वापस आइये** (“Eat and then come back”).  If the abbreviated verb itself is **कर**, the marker is **के**, as in **हम अपना काम करके घर गये** (“After doing our work, we went home”).  The subject is marked by **ने** only if the final verb requires it: **हमने घर जाकर काम किया** (“We went home and worked”).  The abbreviation marker is often omitted entirely, producing forms like **ले आइये** (“take it and come”).  Common verbs in these combinations are **ले जाना** (carry) and **ले चलना** (bring along).  When **कर** is merely understood, both verbs retain their full meanings, and such strings can be ambiguous.  For instance **वह खाना खा गया** may mean **खाना खा कर गया** (“He ate and left”) or **वह सारा खाना खा गया** (“He ate it all up”), where **गया** functions as a clarifier.

**Perfect participle and auxiliaries**

The distinction between the perfect participle by itself and the perfect participle plus a past auxiliary is subtle.  Adding **था** clearly situates the action in the past: **मैं गया था** corresponds to English “I had gone,” but is also used where English simply says “I went.”  A perfect participle without an auxiliary often conveys indefiniteness and is used in questions: **क्या आप गये?** (“Did you go?”).  When the speaker assumes the answer is yes, the auxiliary appears: **आप गये थे न?** (“You did go, didn’t you?”).  The auxiliary is also employed for planned or intended actions that were not carried out, as in **मैं नहीं गया था** (“I didn’t go, after all”).  The present auxiliary **है** indicates a link with the present or very recent past, for example **आपने शादी की है?** (“Have you gotten married?”).  To ask about life experience detached from the present you use the past auxiliary: **शादी की थी?** (“Have you ever married?”).

**Verb agreement rules**

Verbs agree only with a direct‑case expression.  If the subject is in the direct case, the verb agrees with it.  If the subject is oblique (marked by **को** or **ने**), agreement may shift to another direct‑case noun.  When a direct object is present and unmarked by **को**, the verb agrees with that object; if no such expression exists, the verb defaults to the neutral masculine singular form.  Illustrative patterns include:

- **आप यह किताब पढ़ते थे** – here the subject is direct and the verb agrees with **आप**.
- **आपको यह किताब पढ़नी थी** – the subject **आपको** is oblique, so the verb agrees with the feminine object **किताब**.
- **आपने यह किताब पढ़ी थी** – the subject **आपने** is oblique; the verb again agrees with **किताब**.
- **आपने इस किताब को पढ़ा था** – the object **किताब** is marked by **को**; the verb takes the neutral form **पढ़ा**.
- **आपको इस किताब को पढ़ना था** – both subject and object are oblique/marked; the verb remains neutral.

If a verb cannot agree with the subject, it agrees with the nearest direct‑case noun (normally the direct object).  An important exception involves a handful of nouns combined with **करना** – notably **याद** (memory), **पसंद** (liking) and **इस्तेमाल** (use).  These nouns become “transparent” and lose the power to control agreement, allowing a preceding noun to determine the verb form.  For example, **हमने महात्मा जी के शब्द याद किये** (“We remembered his words”) and **हमने अपना पाठ याद किया** (“We memorized our lesson”) show the verb agreeing with the words being remembered rather than with **याद**.  Similarly **इन्होंने आपकी साड़ियां पसंद कीं** (“She liked your saris”) and **इन्होंने हमारे शहर पसंद किये** (“He liked our cities”) show agreement with **साड़ियां** and **शहर**, not with **पसंद**.  In **मैंने ये चीज़ें इस्तेमाल कीं** (“I used these things”) and **मैंने ये कमरा इस्तेमाल किया** (“I used this room”), the verb agrees with **चीज़ें** or **कमरा**, not with **इस्तेमाल**.  When used as ordinary nouns, however, these words control the verb: **आपकी पसंद अच्छी है** (“You have good taste”), **मेरी याद उतनी अच्छी नहीं है** (“My memory isn’t so good”), **अंग्रेज़ी का इस्तेमाल अच्छा नहीं** (“It’s bad to use English”).

These combinations and rules allow you to form more complex sentences while maintaining correct participle usage, possession, verb linking, tense interpretation and agreement in Hindi.
